reason: The hypothesis relies on general corrosion concepts (passive layer, elemental effects) but the cited evidence does not directly support these premises for Q235 steel. E1 describes coating performance on HEAs, not Q235; E2 shows Cr precipitation in a different HEA under salt exposure, but does not link it to passive layer stability or Q235; E3 discusses Ti passive layers in biomaterials, unrelated to Q235 or high-temperature salt environments. None of the cited passages provide specific prior evidence for the key premises as applied to Q235 steel.
premises: Passive layer formation and stability control corrosion protection in Q235 steel
Elemental dissolution, precipitation, and microstructural changes mediate passive layer behavior
High-temperature salt exposure (700–900 °C) can induce microstructural changes that affect protection
Certain alloying elements (e.g., Cr, Ti) enhance passive layer stability and corrosion resistance
Annealing-driven precipitation (e.g., Cr-rich particles) depends on temperature, time, and composition
